checkpoints.description: [1/2] Refuse publish on an archived project (P6, publish half only)

impact_assessment.why: The state-machine inventory's Project row recorded 'publish/check never refuse an archived project'. Verified live: cmd_publish never called is_archived, so `publish` on an archived project ran the whole pipeline and reached a later gate (measured exit 1) instead of refusing. Archiving retires the project, moves it to projects/archive/ and archives the GitHub repository, so publishing one presents a retired project as live.
impact_assessment.benefits: A retired project can no longer be re-published by mistake, and the refusal names the real recovery path (move it out of projects/archive/ and clear the flag), consistent with ADR-400's archive remedy.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: publish gains a refusal, exit 2, before any disk change; check is deliberately unchanged because a read-only audit of an archived project may be legitimate; dependency: none; concurrency: none; state: aikit_cli.py, one test
impact_assessment.mitigation: the guard runs before the pre-push hook is installed, so a refused publish writes nothing; the full TestProjectRegistry class (123 tests) was run to prove no existing publish path regressed

[1/2] Publish the status vocabulary in top-level help as a pointer to the registry, not a copy

impact_assessment.why: P12 proposed copying each machine's states into every --help. Measured first: argparse already publishes ui-id's kinds and archive's flags via choices=, and idea_catcher publishes its statuses, so the premise was largely already delivered. What remained genuinely missing was discoverability of the seven derived vocabularies in status --json, which no --help names. Copying 88 state names into a generated, pinned help string would create a second source of truth for them, the exact drift this audit keeps fixing.
impact_assessment.benefits: One line in --help tells an agent where every vocabulary lives and how to resolve a bare status, without duplicating any of it; the pin also fails if a future change copies a machine's states into the help.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: top-level help text gains an epilog, so aikit_help.py must be regenerated or the ADR-180 pin fails; dependency: none; concurrency: none; state: aikit_parser.py, aikit_help.py, one test
impact_assessment.mitigation: the generated string was rebuilt from the grammar rather than hand-edited, so the pin still proves the fast path matches; the new test asserts the pointer exists and that no machine's states appear verbatim

[1/2] Enforce the idea-status machine on the write path (P5), leaving existing history untouched

impact_assessment.why: The inventory recorded that validate_ideas has no transition table, so a hand-edited register can reopen a terminal row; only Blocked and Superseded were guarded in _apply_status. Measured the blast radius from each idea's own history: 641 real transitions across 1751 ideas, of which exactly 6 violate the documented machine (4x Rejected->Deferred, 1x Superseded->Deferred, 1x Rejected->Integrated). Those 6 are historical rows, so a retroactive validate check would fail the live register for history that cannot be rewritten.
impact_assessment.benefits: A forbidden move through set-status is now refused with the legal targets named, so the register cannot be pushed into a state its own machine does not allow; legal edges are unaffected.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: set-status gains a refusal (exit 1) for moves outside the table; idea_catcher must not import scripts, so the table is declared locally and pinned by a test; existing history is untouched; dependency: none; concurrency: the register write path is unchanged; state: registry.py, 2 tests
impact_assessment.mitigation: the local table was verified byte-identical to the registry before wiring; a test pins them so they cannot drift; all 39 idea_catcher tests pass; the live register still validates, renders and reports exactly the same 133 pre-existing aegean-tge problems and zero aikit ones

[1/2] Pin the new machine-state reader's failure contract with a test

impact_assessment.why: project_machine_states.py is the largest surface this session added and its contract was only verified by my own scratch probe, not by the suite. A fuzz of 40 cases (four state files x eight malformed shapes) found no reader crash, but the specific promise 'an unreadable file becomes a named error, not a guessed state, and the other machines are still reported' was untested.
impact_assessment.benefits: The failure contract is now pinned, so a future edit cannot turn a corrupt media.json into a made-up state or a blanked report.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: additive test only; dependency: none; concurrency: none; state: one test
impact_assessment.mitigation: the test asserts both halves (errors named, readable machines still present); 0.27s for the three status tests; budget gate green at 19.07ms after the host load eased

[1/2] Read a half-restricted project as restricted (P8 read side) so publish --public cannot hand it out

impact_assessment.why: The inventory recorded 'a crash between LICENSE and config reads as unrecorded, and a half-restricted project can be published'. Verified: with the canonical RESTRICTED notice already written to LICENSE and the config record missing, license_state returned unrecorded, and cmd_publish's only restriction check is license_state(...).tier == restricted, so publish --public saw no restriction. The write side of P8 needs a five-write transaction with a migration and rollback test; the read side closes the actual hazard without touching write order.
impact_assessment.benefits: A crash mid-restriction now fails safe: the project reads restricted, so publish --public is refused and status reports the truth instead of 'unrecorded'.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: license_state gains one branch for a LICENSE beginning with the canonical notice header; a blank or third-party LICENSE still reads unrecorded; dependency: none; concurrency: the write path is untouched; state: project_license.py, two tests
impact_assessment.mitigation: the discriminator is the existing RESTRICTED_LICENSE_HEADER constant, not a fuzzy match; all 126 TestProjectRegistry tests and all 11 license-touching classes (348 tests) pass, including the two pins that assert a blank or foreign LICENSE stays unrecorded

[1/2] Make verify_transcript recompute the recorded digests so a replay proves the verdict

impact_assessment.why: The module docstring promises 'a replay can prove the identical verdict', and the machine's own gap admitted verify_transcript never recomputed output_sha. Measured: editing the result output (or even exit_code) left verify_transcript reporting 'transcript ok', and replay_transcript returned a verdict the delegate never produced. The existing tests only covered corrupt JSON, not tampering.
impact_assessment.benefits: A hand-edited transcript now reads as invalid with a Why/Fix naming the field, so replay can no longer assert a verdict the run did not produce; the docstring's promise becomes true.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: verify_transcript gains a failure path; append_result records exit_sha, so a transcript written before it exists is refused as unprovable rather than silently trusted; no AIKit-authored transcript exists yet, so no data migration; dependency: none; concurrency: none; state: delegate_transcript.py, a test, two docs
impact_assessment.mitigation: digests are recomputed with the same _sha the writer used; a falsy-zero bug (exit code 0 hashing as empty) was found by my own test and fixed; all 8 delegate-related test classes pass
